Two steps, and the first one hinges on which silver salt is used.
2-Bromopropane + AgCN, alcoholic, heated.
AgCN is largely covalent, so the lone pair available to attack comes from the **nitrogen**, not
the carbon. The product is therefore the iso cyanide, not the cyanide:
X = (CH₃)₂CH–NC, isopropyl isocyanide.
(Had the reagent been KCN, which is ionic, carbon would have attacked and the product would
have been the nitrile (CH₃)₂CH–CN.)
X + LiAlH₄ — reducing an isocyanide R–NC adds four hydrogens and gives a **secondary** amine,
with a methyl group left on the nitrogen:
Y = (CH₃)₂CH–NH–CH₃
Name it: the longer chain on N is propane with the amine at C2, and a methyl sits on nitrogen.
∴ N-methylpropan-2-amine.

kcet|Chemistry|2015|8||0|0.s:
First identify the gas. White phosphorus warmed with concentrated NaOH in an inert
atmosphere disproportionates:
P₄ + 3NaOH + 3H₂O ⇒ PH₃ + 3NaH₂PO₂
The gas is phosphine, PH₃. (The CO₂ atmosphere is there to keep air out, because PH₃ traces
ignite spontaneously.)
Now test the statements.
(3) True — PH₃ is very poisonous and smells of rotten fish or garlic.
(4) True — its aqueous solution decomposes in light, giving red phosphorus and hydrogen.
(1) True and (2) false — PH₃ is a **weaker** base than NH₃. Phosphorus is larger than nitrogen,
so its lone pair occupies a bigger, more diffuse 3s orbital and is less available for donation to
a proton. Basicity falls down the group: NH₃ > PH₃ > AsH₃ > SbH₃ > BiH₃.
∴ statement (2) is incorrect.

kcet|Chemistry|2015|10||0|0.s:
Isotonic solutions have equal osmotic pressure, and since π = CRT at the same temperature,
that simply means equal molar concentration.
Urea: 0.06% w/v means 0.06 g in 100 mL, which is 0.6 g per litre.
Molar mass of urea, NH₂CONH₂ = 60 g mol⁻¹
concentration = 0.6 / 60 = 0.01 mol L⁻¹
So the glucose solution must also be 0.01 M, which option (3) states directly.
For the w/v options: 0.01 M glucose (M = 180) is 1.8 g L⁻¹, that is 0.18% w/v — neither 0.06%
nor 0.6%, so (1) and (2) are both wrong.
Neither solute dissociates, so i = 1 for both and no van't Hoff correction is needed.
∴ 0.01 M glucose solution.

kcet|Chemistry|2015|11||0|0:
Express the fraction remaining as a power of a half.
12.5% = 12.5/100 = 1/8 = (1/2)³
So three half-lives have passed.
That took one hour:
3 × t½ = 60 min
t½ = 20 min
Check it through: 100% ⇒ 50% at 20 min ⇒ 25% at 40 min ⇒ 12.5% at 60 min ✓
The question asks when the reaction was half completed, which is one half-life.
For a first order reaction the half-life does not depend on the starting concentration, so this
is a fixed 20 minutes whatever you began with.
∴ 20 minutes.
kcet|Chemistry|2015|12||0|0:
The flocculation value is the minimum concentration of electrolyte needed to coagulate a sol,
so the **maximum** flocculation value belongs to the **least effective** electrolyte.
AgI/Ag⁺ means the sol was made with silver nitrate in excess, so the particles adsorb Ag⁺ and
the sol is **positively charged**.
A positive sol is coagulated by the negative ion of the electrolyte, so compare the anions.
By the Hardy–Schulze rule, coagulating power rises steeply with the charge on that ion:
PO₄³⁻ > SO₄²⁻ ≈ S²⁻ > Cl⁻
Cl⁻ carries only one negative charge, so NaCl is the weakest coagulant here and needs the
highest concentration — the maximum flocculation value.
∴ NaCl.

kcet|Chemistry|2015|14||0|0.s:
Geometrical isomerism needs two or more ways of arranging the ligands in space that cannot
be interconverted by rotating the whole molecule.
Tetrahedral complexes show none at all. Every vertex of a tetrahedron is adjacent to every
other, so there is no cis and no trans — that rules out (2) and (4) immediately.
MA₃B square planar: the single B can go to any corner, but all four corners of a square are
equivalent by rotation, so there is only one arrangement. No isomerism.
MABCD square planar: here the four ligands all differ, and the isomer is decided by which
ligand sits **opposite** A. B, C or D can each take that position, giving three distinct isomers.
So only the square planar MABCD qualifies.
∴ MABCD – square planar.

kcet|Chemistry|2015|15||0|0.s:
Gadolinium has Z = 64. Its configuration is one of the irregular ones:
Gd = [Xe] 4f⁷ 5d¹ 6s²
The 5d¹ appears because a half-filled 4f⁷ subshell is especially stable, so the last electron goes
to 5d rather than pairing up in 4f.
Now form Gd²⁺. For any transition or inner-transition element the outermost **s** electrons are
removed first, before d or f.
Remove the two 6s electrons:
Gd²⁺ = [Xe] 4f⁷ 5d¹
Note this keeps both the stable half-filled 4f⁷ and the lone 5d electron.
The common error is option (2), [Xe]4f⁷, which comes from removing the 5d electron as well —
that would be Gd³⁺, the usual oxidation state of the lanthanoids.
∴ [Xe] 4f⁷ 5d¹.

kcet|Chemistry|2015|16||0|0.s:
Follow the qualitative analysis.
MSO₄ + NH₄OH gives a **white** precipitate. That rules out copper (pale blue), iron (dirty green
or brown) and leaves zinc or aluminium:
ZnSO₄ + 2NH₄OH ⇒ Zn(OH)₂↓ (white) + (NH₄)₂SO₄
X + **excess** NH₄OH dissolves. This is the deciding step. Zn(OH)₂ is soluble in excess ammonia
because it forms a soluble ammine complex:
Zn(OH)₂ + 4NH₄OH ⇒ [Zn(NH₃)₄](OH)₂ + 4H₂O
Al(OH)₃ does **not** dissolve in excess ammonia, so aluminium is eliminated.
Y + H₂S gives a precipitate: the complex is broken down and zinc sulphide is thrown out:
[Zn(NH₃)₄]²⁺ + H₂S ⇒ ZnS↓ (white) + 2NH₄⁺ + 2NH₃
∴ M is Zn and Z is ZnS.

kcet|Chemistry|2015|17||0|0.s:
2-Bromobutane, CH₃CHBrCH₂CH₃, has four different groups on C2 — H, Br, CH₃ and C₂H₅ — so
that carbon is a stereocentre and the compound is optically active.
Hydrolysis with aqueous NaOH on a secondary halide proceeds substantially by SN1:
Step 1 — the C–Br bond ionises, giving a secondary carbocation. That carbocation is sp²
hybridised and therefore **planar**, so the stereochemical information is lost.
Step 2 — OH⁻ attacks, and it can approach either face of the flat carbocation with equal ease.
Attack from one face gives the (+) alcohol, from the other the (−) alcohol, in equal amounts.
Equal amounts of the two enantiomers make a racemic mixture, written (±), which is optically
inactive because the rotations cancel.
The chain is unchanged, so the product is butan-2-ol, not butan-1-ol.
∴ (±) butan-2-ol.
